It forecasts an unborrowed position by year end, due to the High Needs Stability Grant and business rates from new Teesworks businesses.
findings.matters: A council forecasting to be unborrowed at year end, after borrowing rose in the half year, is relevant to lenders' exposure to the council.

findings.headline: Business rates Collection Fund deficit of £11.403m at Quarter 2, down from £12.395m at Quarter 1, with the council's 49% share at £5.587m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the deficit to a worsening 2025/26 outturn, reduced liability from rateable value changes and reliefs, and higher appeal and bad debt provisions. The shortfall in retained rates is to be met by safety net grant, transferred to a reserve for the 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: The deficit is being carried into 2027/28 and is partly covered by a safety net grant reserve, so the council's share of the shortfall depends on how that reserve is used.

findings.headline: DSG deficit predicted to rise by £10.385m to £12.493m by 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The paper says the deficit is predicted to increase further in 2026/27, and it awaits Government detail on support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28. It also says the statutory override now runs to 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: Deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 are not yet covered by announced Government support, and the override date is the period lenders would look at for DSG exposure.
findings.figures: £10.385m predicted increase; £12.493m forecast deficit at 31 March 2027; 31 March 2028 override end date
findings.quote: The DSG deficit is predicted to further increase by £10.385 million to £12.493 million by 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Stability Grant of £18.975m to reduce the DSG deficit accrued to end 2025/26 from £21.083m to £2.108m
findings.detail: The grant follows approval of the council's SEND reform plan and is due on 30 November 2026. The paper says the grant will reduce the deficit, though a further £10.385m is forecast to be added in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This shows the Government's stabilisation mechanism for DSG High Needs deficits applied in practice, and the paper sets out the residual deficit the council must meet from its own resources in 2028/29.
findings.figures: £18.975m High Needs Stability Grant; £21.083m deficit at end 2025/26; £2.108m residual deficit; 30 November 2026 receipt date

findings.headline: Asset-sale capital receipts used to fund transformation are forecast at £0.500m against a £2.000m budget
findings.detail: The paper says a number of larger disposals are taking longer than originally anticipated and are no longer expected to complete this year. Spending on transformation projects is being reduced to match the lower receipts, and further disposals may still arise in year.
findings.matters: Capital receipts used to fund revenue-linked transformation are slipping, and the paper says some sales involve income-generating assets that may be kept.
findings.figures: £2.000m budgeted receipts flexibility; £0.500m now projected receipts; £1.500m outstanding; £0.253m achieved; £0.247m in progress

findings.detail: The text gives £1.622m achieved (36%) and £2.186m outstanding. The summary table in paragraph 4.24 gives £1.083m achieved (24%), £0.471m in progress and £2.960m outstanding, so the text and table do not agree. The outstanding amount is mainly £1.500m of capital receipts not expected this year and £1.456m of children's placement savings now largely expected in future years.
findings.matters: Savings are a core part of the plan to contain the overspend, and the paper's two sets of achieved and outstanding figures differ.

findings.quote: £1.622 million of these savings have been classified as being achieved (36%)

findings.headline: Health care income forecast at 6.62% of Residential and Supported Accommodation spend, against 11.72% in 2021/22
findings.detail: The paper forecasts £2.735m of health income against £41.312m total expenditure in these areas. It compares this with £0.798m against £6.804m in 2021/22 and says health funding is failing to keep pace with the cost of these placements.
findings.matters: A falling share of health funding leaves the council carrying more of the cost of high-need placements, and other councils face the same NHS contribution arrangements.

findings.headline: Children and Families forecasts an £8.232m overspend, with 111.8 young people in Residential and Supported Accommodation against 100.7 budgeted
findings.detail: The overspend is driven by Residential (£7.936m) and Supported Accommodation (£0.304m) placements. The paper attributes £3.5m to volume and a further £4.8m to rising average placement costs, which it gives as £0.375m for Residential and £0.352m for Supported Accommodation.
findings.matters: Children's social care placement costs are the main driver of the overspend, and the paper shows both the number of placements and the unit cost rising.
findings.figures: £8.232m Children and Families forecast overspend; 100.7 budgeted average young people; 111.8 Q2 average young people; £3.5m volume pressure; £4.8m cost pressure; £0.375m Residential average cost; £0.352m Supported Accommodation average cost
findings.quote: This is driving a volume pressure of circa £3.5 million.

findings.headline: Q2 forecast year-end net overspend of £7.448m, up from £5.647m at Quarter 1
findings.detail: The Quarter 2 forecast shows a net overspend of £7.448m after the £2.000m flexible use of capital receipts is reduced to £0.500m. Children and Families is forecasting £8.232m over budget, offset in part by a £4.115m underspend in Corporate Allocations.
findings.matters: Overspend is rising against the Q1 forecast, and the paper says it will be funded from increased EFS because reserves are low, so the cost falls on a single directorate.
findings.figures: £7.448m Q2 net overspend; £5.647m Q1 forecast; £1.801m change; £8.232m Children and Families; £4.115m Corporate Allocations underspend
findings.quote: As at Quarter 2 2026/27, the Council is forecasting a year-end net overspend of £7.448 million.

findings.headline: Government's treatment of the September 2026 CPI rate of 3.5% is identified as a key uncertainty for 2027/28 funding
findings.detail: The paper says the September 2026 CPI rate of 3.5% is significantly higher than the inflation assumptions in the multi-year settlement. Business rates baselines are expected to be uplifted by the higher CPI rate, but overall funding allocations are expected to remain cash-limited with compensating adjustments through Revenue Support Grant. The provisional settlement is expected in late December.
findings.matters: Whether the Government compensates councils for the higher CPI uplift is a question that affects every council's 2027/28 funding position.
findings.figures: 3.5% September 2026 CPI rate; 3.9% National Living Wage increase from April 2027
findings.quote: A key uncertainty for 2027/28 is how the Government will treat the September 2026 CPI rate of 3.5%

findings.headline: Capital programme of £275.649 million to 2031/32, with borrowing of £74.220 million plus £99.164 million of EFS borrowing
findings.detail: The paper says the indicative funding for the programme is £97.948 million of grant funding, £74.220 million of borrowing, £99.164 million of EFS borrowing, £4.250 million of capital receipts and £0.067 million from revenue. It also says approximately £1.32 of external funding is leveraged for every £1 borrowed, excluding EFS borrowing.
findings.matters: The split between grant, prudential borrowing and EFS-funded borrowing shows how much of the capital programme depends on borrowing, which is the figure a lender will want to see.

findings.headline: MTFS reserve forecast at £7.693 million in 2027/28 and £3.508 million in 2028/29, before being replenished
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS reserve will remain at current levels for 2027/28, then be used to offset the forecast residual DSG deficit in 2028/29, and be replenished in the last two years of the MTFS. The business rates volatility reserve is forecast to rise from £5.261 million in 2027/28 to £9.261 million from 2029/30.
findings.matters: A drawdown from the MTFS reserve to absorb the DSG deficit, followed by a planned rebuild, is a reserve position a finance director would compare against their own minimum resilience level.

findings.headline: Council states the 2026/27 funding formula assesses its relative need below its rate of children in care
findings.detail: The paper says the funding formula introduced from 2026/27 assesses the council's relative need at a lower level than its rate of children in care, creating a material gap between available funding and expenditure requirements. The paper attributes this to the prolonged delay in national funding reform.
findings.matters: A funding formula that is judged to understate need for children in care is an issue other councils with similar demographics will be tracking through the Fair Funding Reform.
findings.figures: No figure given in the paper for the gap
findings.quote: assesses the Council's relative need at a significantly lower level than its rate of children in care

findings.headline: Children in care demographic and cost pressure of £8.000 million in 2027/28, within £33.191 million of total service investments
findings.detail: The paper says the increase in the cost base carried into 2027/28 is mainly owing to the pressures experienced on children in care and adult social care costs. The children in care pressure is the largest single service investment in the table, and the paper calls children's care placements the council's most significant financial pressure.
findings.matters: Children's social care placement costs are a common source of overspend across councils, and the scale of the investment shows the size of the demand pressure in this council.

findings.headline: Transformation savings planned at £4.607 million in 2027/28, falling to £2.544 million in 2028/29
findings.detail: The planned savings include £2.000 million from children in care transformation plans in 2027/28, £2.000 million from utilising asset sales proceeds through the flexible use of capital receipts in 2027/28, and £0.585 million from in-borough children's care partnership placements. The savings total falls to £1.570 million in 2029/30 and £1.222 million in 2030/31.
findings.matters: The mix of savings, with a large share from children in care and asset sales, is what a peer council or lender would test against the stated pressures.

findings.headline: Council reports delivering more than £22 million of savings over the past five years
findings.detail: The paper cites more than £22 million of savings delivered over five years through efficiency and transformation initiatives. It also cites £1.5 million of savings delivered in home to school transport through enhanced governance, operational processes and contract management.
findings.matters: A track record of delivered savings is the evidence a lender or peer council uses to judge whether the new transformation savings are credible.
findings.figures: more than £22 million savings over five years; £1.5 million home to school transport savings
findings.quote: the Council has delivered more than £22 million of savings over the past five years

findings.detail: The first major Teesworks projects have been assessed by the Valuation Office Agency, and the paper says the rateable values are broadly in line with the MTFS assumptions. The paper also notes the projections depend on the timing and delivery of developments and on the yield determined by the Valuation Office, and that some of the forecast depends on developments still under construction.
findings.matters: Business rates growth from a single regeneration site is a large share of the forecast, so whether valuations match assumptions is a question peer councils with similar schemes will also be watching.
findings.quote: is forecast to deliver business rates for the council of £13.2 million in 2027/28, rising to £48.7 million by 2031/32

findings.matters: The gap between the total collection fund deficit and the council's share shows how the deficit is being shared with other precepting authorities, which matters to finance officers comparing collection performance.

Government will fund the retained-rates shortfall through safety net grant, transferred into a reserve to fund the in-year deficit. The residual deficit carried forward from 2025/26 must be addressed in the 2027/28 MTFS refresh.
findings.matters: Business rates collection fund deficits and safety net funding are a common pressure point across councils, and the split between in-year and carried-forward amounts affects how it is funded.

findings.quote: For business rates, the total deficit is forecast at £11.403 million.

findings.headline: Residual DSG deficit forecast at £4.185 million by 2028/29, with the statutory override for DSG deficits expiring on 31 March 2028
findings.detail: Government has provided 90% grant support for DSG deficits accrued to the end of 2025/26 and has indicated similar support for the following two years. The paper says that after the override expires Government will take the financial risk away from councils. The residual DSG deficit, after assuming 90% grant support in 2026/27 and 2027/28, is forecast at £4.185 million by 2028/29.
findings.matters: The date the DSG override ends and the residual balance left with the council are the two figures a lender or peer finance officer needs to judge exposure to SEND-driven deficits.

findings.matters: The forecast gap sits in the two years after the proposed budget, so the scale of the planned EFS dependence through 2029/30 is visible to any reader assessing the plan's credibility.

findings.headline: Redcar and Cleveland's provisional Exceptional Financial Support requirement for 2027/28 is £25.820 million
findings.detail: The paper says the initial assessment of the 2027/28 budget gap has informed a provisional EFS requirement, and that the estimate is based on current assumptions. It also says the application and approval timetable is expected to follow 2026/27, and that Government flexibility remains necessary in the early years of the plan.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, will want to know the size of the Government support the budget depends on and whether the timetable for approving it is on track.

findings.detail: The paper says planning fees are still set nationally with CPI-linked increases capped at 10%, but locally set fees will need to reflect the authority's costs and income will be kept for planning. The detailed arrangements are still being developed.
findings.matters: Once in force, locally set planning fees would change how every planning authority recovers costs, so the detailed regulations will matter to finance teams across England.
findings.figures: CPI-linked annual increase cap: 10%
findings.quote: providing powers for Local Planning Authorities (LPAs) to set their own planning

findings.headline: Public Rights of Way charges are being restructured and the opposed-order charge is proposed to be removed, with four current fees replaced.
findings.detail: The service found its fees did not reflect the work involved. The paper says the extent of work and legal costs from objections cannot be reliably predicted, so the opposed-order charge goes. New fees include £250 for 5-day and 21-day Traffic Regulation Order applications, £450 for 6-month and extension applications, and £1,100 for unopposed public path orders.
findings.matters: A council removing a fee because its cost cannot be predicted, and replacing it with fixed charges, shows one way to address cost recovery on legal processes that other councils may face.

findings.matters: Any council recovering council tax through liability orders will see this fee cut and the cost-recovery gap widen, so the national cap affects revenue across the sector.

findings.headline: Kirkleatham Museum adult admission is proposed to rise from £3 to £5.00, with family admission at £12.00.
findings.detail: Admission charges were introduced at Kirkleatham in 2025/26. The paper says the service benchmarked against Preston Park Museum (£12 adult annual admission) and Ryedale Folk Museum (£12 adult admission), and proposes a revised structure that keeps unlimited return visits for 12 months.
findings.matters: It is a visible step-up in a newly introduced charge, and the benchmarking basis is one peer councils with museum charges can compare against.

findings.headline: Cemetery fees are proposed to stay at 2026/27 levels because cemeteries income has been flat for four years.
findings.detail: The paper links flat income to residents possibly choosing cheaper alternatives to traditional burial. It says a further price rise, even by inflation, would likely worsen the drop in income while maintenance costs keep rising, and it calls for a cemeteries strategy.
findings.matters: A council that has decided price rises would reduce income in a service where costs are rising is a case other councils with similar bereavement services will recognise.

findings.detail: The paper says the car parking approach changed for 2025/26 from an across-the-board inflationary increase to a different model. Cabinet is now proposing to hold fees at the 2025/26 level.
findings.matters: Holding a fee line that other charges are uplifted by RPI is a direct choice to forgo inflation-linked income in a year when the paper says the council needs more income.
findings.figures: RPI uplift for April 2026: 2.9%
findings.quote: It is proposed by Cabinet to retain car parking fees at the 2025/26 levels for 2027/28.

findings.detail: The paper cites the CIPFA Financial Resilience Index and says the council's share was broadly comparable to 6.98% in 2023/24 and 6.66% in 2022/23. It attributes the low share to deprivation-driven service demand and limited scope to raise charges.
findings.matters: A finance director at a peer council can benchmark their own charging share against this, and a lender can see the structural limit on the council's self-generated income.
findings.quote: The index shows that the Council generates the lowest level of fees and charges income as a proportion of service expenditure amongst its statistical neighbour group, with a highest figure of 14.18%.

findings.matters: £6m allocation against 'critically low' reserves over a multi-year period confirms severe reserve depletion and indicates incremental recovery will take years, leaving the council at heightened risk in the interim

findings.headline: Children in care numbered 431 as at 22 June 2026, fluctuating between 410-450 over six months, driving sustained budget pressures
findings.detail: The council continues to experience significant budget pressures driven by increasing numbers of children in care requiring high-cost placements. findings.matters: Children's social care is a statutory service where underfunding creates safeguarding risks and failure to meet demand. High-cost placement inflation is the primary budget pressure and transformation activity shows no resolution in sight
findings.figures: 431 children in care as at 22 June 2026; numbers fluctuating between 410-450 across last 6 months; £3m capital investment plus £2m transformational investment allocated

This is explicitly described as supporting the authority facing acute financial challenges where a path to sustainability exists, but indicates inability to close the gap independently.
findings.matters: Reliance on exceptional government support demonstrates the council cannot achieve financial balance through its own resources or savings, raising questions about underlying structural sustainability
findings.figures: £18.4m exceptional financial support required for 2026/27

The scheme supports Authority's facing acute financial challenges in bridging short-term budget gaps, where a path to sustainability exists. The Authority has planned to utilise £18.4m of EFS to support the balancing of its 2026/27 Budget

findings.headline: Council debt increased to £247.069m from £225.864m in Q3; now in overborrowing position of £9.685m against Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: Debt rose by £21.2m in final quarter (Q4) due to £27.5m new PWLB loans and £2.5m local authority loan, less repayment instalments. The council's Capital Financing Requirement is £289.205m (adjusted to £237.384m for PFI/lease liabilities), but actual borrowing is £247.069m, creating an overborrowing position of £9.685m. This breaches the CFR but remains within the authorised operational limit. The overborrowing is primarily attributable to the DSG deficit (£21.083m), which should reverse once the government's High Needs Stability Grant is received (pending SEND reform plan approval).
findings.matters: An overborrowing position is technically a prudential code breach (even if within authorised limits) and creates contingent refinancing risk if the DSG grant does not materialise as expected. The council has deliberately borrowed more than its CFR to manage the DSG deficit impact.
findings.figures: Total debt £247.069m (up from £225.864m in Q3); CFR £289.205m (adjusted £237.384m); overborrowing £9.685m; new PWLB loans £27.5m; local authority loan £2.5m; DSG deficit £21.083m
findings.quote: When this is compared to the Council's borrowing of £247.069 million this results in an overborrowing position of £9.685 million. The main driver of this over borrowed position is the DSG deficit of £21.083 million referenced within this report. It is anticipated that once the local SEND reform plan is secured, c£18.975 million of our forecast 2025/26-year end deficit should be addressed via the High Needs Stability Grant reversing this over borrowed position.

findings.headline: Council approved £3.5m additional capital borrowing for ERP system replacement with current system end-of-life by 30 September 2027
findings.detail: The council's current Enterprise Resource Planning system (supporting HR, finance, payroll, procurement) expires on 30 September 2027 and cannot be extended. A comprehensive options appraisal identified replacement as unavoidable and time-critical. The preferred solution (Option 3) involves £3.5 million capital investment funded via borrowing, with implementation by the supplier's in-house team (claimed 95% on-time, on-budget delivery track record). Revenue costs will be met from existing transformation budgets.
findings.matters: An aging, non-extensible critical system creates binary risk: borrow now and replace on schedule, or face operational failure post-September 2027. A lender needs assurance that implementation is realistic; the council rejected Option 2 partly due to third-party implementation partner risk.
findings.figures: £3.5m capital investment; 15-year financing period; system end-of-life 30 September 2027; Option 3 chosen over Option 1 (£2.8m, current supplier) and Option 2 (£3.25m, third-party implementation risk)
findings.quote: The Council is required to replace its existing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system, which supports critical financial, human resources, payroll and procurement functions, ahead of the expiry of the current contract on 30 September 2027. This report therefore seeks approval for an additional £3.5m of capital investment, funded through borrowing, to support the implementation of a new ERP system.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £1.784m; winter pressures and hospital discharge delays driving residential placement demand
findings.detail: Adult and Community Services overspent by £1.784 million, primarily due to increased demand for residential care. The paper specifically cites impact of 2025 winter pressures and hospital discharge arrangements, noting that some patients placed in short-term residential beds became permanent residents. Actions taken include changes to hospital discharge pathways and investment in hospital social work resource, and the trend has "levelled out".
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is structural and will intensify with demographic change. An overspend driven by hospital discharge suggests systemic rather than temporary pressures, and control measures appear reactive rather than preventive.
findings.figures: £1.784m overspend in Adult and Community Services
findings.quote: The Directorate have incurred an overspend of £1.784 million versus budget. The majority of the overspend related to increased demand for residential care, with the impact of the 2025 winter pressures still impacting as well as hospitals in crisis exasperating volume pressures nationally as well as here in Redcar and Cleveland.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased £8.628m to cumulative £21.083m; statutory override expires 2028 with no funded solution yet confirmed
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block deficit grew significantly from £12.455m to £21.083m. The council operates under a statutory override that isolates this from usable reserves, but that override expires 31 March 2028. Government has committed to resolving 90% of deficits accrued to end-2025/26 via a High Needs Stability Grant (subject to council approval of a local SEND reform plan), but the remaining 10% and any post-2028 deficits have no confirmed funding source.
findings.matters: Although currently ring-fenced by statute, this deficit will crystallise as a real financial liability post-2028 unless government assumptions about demand change dramatically. The council cannot control SEND placement demand directly, creating medium-term budget risk.
findings.figures: 2024/25 DSG deficit £12.455m; 2025/26 deficit increase £8.628m; end-of-year deficit £21.083m; government to resolve ~£18.975m (90%) via Stability Grant if SEND reform plan approved; statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The DSG deficit has increased by a further £8.628 million in 2025/26 to an overall deficit of £21.083 million as at 31 March 2026. The increasing pressure in DSG, and in particular the High Needs Block, is because alongside social care, education services are experiencing an increase in more complex placements requiring a place in special schools.

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell 10% in year: from £17.628m to £15.997m, with MTFS Reserve drawn down £1.309m despite approved top-up
findings.detail: The council drew down £1.309 million from the Medium-Term Financial Strategy Reserve during 2025/26 to fund the overspend position, despite an approved £0.936 million top-up in the February 2025 budget. Overall reserves declined by approximately 10% across the year. The council held back some mitigating measures by using in-year underspends and release of other reserves, but the underlying trajectory is negative.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to future shocks. A 10% annual drawdown at this scale is unsustainable and signals the council is consuming rather than building resilience.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £17.628m; closing reserves £15.997m; MTFS Reserve drawdown £1.309m; approved top-up £0.936m; total year reduction £1.631m (10%)
findings.quote: The approved 2025/26 Budget included a £0.936 million top-up to the MTFS Reserve. However, a combination of factors, such as delays in delivering all planned transformation savings and the continuing in-year pressures contributing to the 2025/26 overspend of £2.412 million, mean that the Council has needed to draw down £1.309 million of the MTFS Reserve during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Transformation Programme delivered only 52% of planned £8.848m savings; £4.208m of savings unachieved
findings.detail: The council achieved £4.640 million of planned transformation savings but missed £4.208 million (48%). The majority of unachieved balance relates to asset sales (£2.332 million shortfall) and delays in developing in-house children's care placements (£1.780 million of £2.918 million saving unachieved). Both initiatives remain ongoing and are expected to deliver in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Failed transformation programmes signal operational execution risk and can cascade into future budget failures if assumed savings do not materialise. Asset sale delays in particular can reflect either market conditions or organisational capability constraints.
findings.figures: £8.848m planned savings; £4.640m achieved (52%); £4.208m not achieved (48%); asset sales shortfall £2.332m; children's placements in-house development shortfall £1.780m
findings.quote: The Transformation Programme sought to deliver planned savings of £8.848 million in 2025/26. In summary £4.640 million of these savings have been classified as being achieved (52%) and £4.208 million (48%) were not achieved. The majority of the unachieved balance relates to the sale of fixed assets and savings from the development of in-house children's care placements.

findings.headline: Collection Fund: council tax swung to £1.164m deficit (council share £0.967m); business rates to £2.232m deficit (council share £1.094m) in final quarter
findings.detail: Council tax collection fund shifted £1.805 million from Q3 position due to increased discounts and exemptions plus higher bad debt provisions. Business rates swung £1.552 million due to Teesworks income delays, a large hereditament appeal success, and increased appeals provisions in the final quarter. The council's retained share is £0.967m (council tax) and £1.094m (business rates), totalling £2.061m of deficits to be managed.
findings.matters: A deteriorating collection fund signals either structural challenges in the tax base or forecast accuracy issues, both material to lender confidence. The sharp Q4 movement suggests risk management gaps and the impact feeds directly into 2027/28 budget planning.
findings.figures: Council tax: £1.164m deficit (council share £0.967m); business rates: £2.232m deficit (council share £1.094m); council tax Q3-to-outturn swing £1.805m; business rates swing £1.552m
findings.quote: For council tax, the total year-end deficit as referenced in Appendix 1 is £1.164 million (compared to a surplus of £0.641 million in Quarter 3). The Council retains an 83% share of this deficit, which equates to £0.967million. This worsened year-end position has arisen due an increase in discounts and exemptions which has lowered the overall income into the Collection Fund.

findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £7.132m driven by high-cost residential placements hitting £8.452m over budget
findings.detail: Children in care placement costs totalled £43.779 million against a budget expectation, with residential and supported accommodation placements alone £7.172 million over budget. The council placed an average of 96.6 children in these high-cost settings, rising to 104 by end of March 2026. Each placement costs approximately £0.322 million annually. The overspend reflects both rising numbers and increasing complexity of children's needs.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial sustainability needs to understand whether this is a one-off or structural demand pressure; children's services is typically the most volatile budget and this overspend consumed most of the year's total variance.
findings.figures: £43.779 million actual vs budget; £8.452 million overspend; £7.172 million on residential/supported accommodation alone; average 96.6 children, peak 104; £0.322 million per placement per annum
findings.quote: Children in our care placement costs were £43.779 million, which was £8.452 million higher than budget (£7.438 million higher at Q3). The worsening position relates to the increased number and cost of children in high-cost placements, specifically residential and supported accommodation, which was £7.172 million (£6.060 million at Q3).

findings.headline: A £2.918m transformation savings target for in-borough children's placements is only 44% delivered, with more than half still outstanding
findings.detail: The council targeted £2.918m in savings from developing more in-borough placements for children in care. By year-end, only £1.291m (44%) was achieved, with £1.627m (56%) carried forward. The council attributes this to Ofsted approval delays rather than plan failure, but the shortfall remains.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing deficit management needs to know whether savings plans are on track. This plan is significantly behind. If not recovered in 2026/27, it signals the council's savings forecast was too optimistic.
findings.figures: £2.918m target; £1.291m (44%) achieved; £1.627m (56%) unachieved as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: There was a target for 2025/26 of £2.918m. As at 31 March 2026, £1.291m (44%) had been achieved with £1.627m (56%) still to achieve.

findings.headline: Children's social work recruitment remains unresolved, forcing continued reliance on agency workers costing £0.990m despite falling from the prior year
findings.detail: The council holds social work vacancies as a cost control, creating £1.119m in staffing underspend. However, this forces use of agency workers at £0.990m. Agency costs have fallen from £1.446m in 2024/25, suggesting some improvement, but the council still cannot recruit to its permanent establishment.
findings.matters: Persistent recruitment failure in a critical service is a risk indicator. The council is managing cost by understaffing and using agency workers, which is neither sustainable nor cost-effective long-term.
findings.figures: £0.990m agency spend in 2025/26; £1.446m in 2024/25 (32% reduction); £1.119m underspend from staffing vacancies
findings.quote: Staffing costs across all social worker areas were £0.129m lower than budget. There were total staffing savings of £1.119m, created from the holding of vacancies. This represents the difficulties of recruiting still being experienced in the market.

findings.headline: Independent and Non-Maintained Special Schools placements have more than doubled in four years, driving a £5.073m overspend with no corresponding budget increase
findings.detail: INMSS placements grew from 68 children in 2020/21 to 165 in 2025/26 (142.7% increase), while average cost per place rose 31.2% from £0.050m to £0.066m. The budget did not grow in line with this demand; despite a £2.929m overspend in 2024/25, it remained largely unchanged for 2025/26.
findings.matters: This is a sustained, accelerating demand that the council cannot fund. It is the largest single pressure in the High Needs Block and will recur annually without external intervention or funding reform.
findings.figures: 165 children vs 68 in 2020/21 (142.7% increase); average cost £0.066m in 2025/26 vs £0.050m in 2020/21 (31.2% increase); £5.073m overspend
findings.quote: The number of children within these placements has increased over the same period from 68 to 165 which is an increase of 142.7%.

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit has accumulated to £21.083m and is ring-fenced, requiring it to be carried forward indefinitely
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £8.628m in 2025/26, adding to a £12.455m prior-year carry-forward. The total £21.083m deficit must be carried forward because DSG is ring-fenced. The council's SEND Reform Plan could reduce this by £18.975m (90% reduction) if approved, but depends on a Schools White Paper not yet released and expires as a reserve override on 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: An accumulated £21m liability is material. It signals the High Needs Block is fundamentally under-resourced. The council's solution depends on external approval and has an expiry date, creating an uncertain tail risk.
findings.figures: £21.083m total DSG deficit (£12.455m prior year + £8.628m 2025/26); £18.975m expected reduction from reform plan if approved; override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: DSG is a ring-fenced grant and as such this year-end deficit balance is carried forward to the next financial year. The balance from the previous year end is £12.455m creating a total deficit at the end of 25/26 of £21.083m.

findings.headline: Children's placement costs overran by £8.452m, driven by 27 more children in care and 24 more high-cost residential placements than budgeted
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 376 children in care but had an average of 403. High-cost residential placements rose from 73 budgeted to 97 actual, at an average cost of £0.322m per child. The overspend worsened by £1.016m in Q4 alone, signalling an unresolved structural pressure.
findings.matters: A lender must know whether this is a one-off or a structural gap in budget forecasting. These are uncontrollable demand drivers that repeat annually and erode council reserves.
findings.figures: 403 children vs 376 budgeted; 97 residential placements vs 73 budgeted; £0.322m average cost per residential place; £8.452m total overspend; £1.016m worsening in Q4
findings.quote: The Budget for 2025/26 was built on the Council having an average of 376 children in its care over the financial year. The actual average was significantly higher with 403 children in our care.

findings.headline: Management is building reserves specifically to hedge against EU trade deal impacts and 2027 legislative changes, signalling concern about future financial stability.
findings.detail: The Authority is requesting approval to transfer a £128,543 underspend to reserves 'to help mitigate the continued risks associated with the transition to a Target Operating Model (TOM), expected future legislative changes (planned for 2027) any other unforeseen costs'. The report explicitly notes that clarity on the EU trade deal impact will be provided later, and reserves are being built to provide 'resilience versus potential adverse changes'.
findings.matters: This indicates management anticipates material adverse impacts from trade policy or legislative change, creating downside risk to the Authority's finances and to Redcar and Cleveland's own budget if costs or contributions must increase.
findings.figures: Reserves carried forward £511,986 (up from £380,414); underspend transfer £128,543; cash in hand £508,035
findings.quote: Approve the transfer of an underspend of £128,543 achieved in 2025/26, to reserves for carry-forward and use in 2026/27, to help mitigate the continued risks associated with the transition to a Target Operating Model (TOM), expected future legislative changes (planned for 2027) any other unforeseen costs.

findings.paper_title: RTPHA Financial Position 2025-26 Unaudited accounts report final
findings.headline: Nearly £160k of the income surplus came from animal health checks that were largely unknown and dependent on external EU disease events.
findings.detail: The Authority budgeted for £660,500 in income but received £825,440, creating a variance of £164,940. Of this, £159,916 came from 'additional product of animal origin income (£159,916 additional) which was largely unknown'. This income is tied to increased disease checks following EU animal outbreaks and is not a recurring revenue stream that can be relied upon.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to assess whether funding is stable; income dependent on external disease prevalence could reverse, creating sudden budget pressure on Redcar and Cleveland, which contributes £81,978 to the Authority.
findings.figures: Income variance £164,940; animal-origin income £159,916; total income £825,440 vs budget £660,500
findings.quote: Income - £164,940 more than budget primarily as a result of additional product of animal origin income (£159,916 additional) which was largely unknown.

findings.headline: Council identifies £7.172m new savings across medium-term financial strategy after delivering over £20m in previous four years
findings.detail: Despite four years of delivering over £20 million in savings, the council has identified only £7.172 million in new savings across the entire medium-term financial strategy. The document explicitly states 'the scope for further efficiencies is constrained' and the savings programme has been 'deliberately targeted and proportionate' given previous extensive programmes. This limited savings capacity means the council has minimal ability to address unexpected cost pressures or demand spikes beyond what the budget already assumes.
findings.matters: When a council cannot find meaningful additional savings despite acute financial pressure, it signals that service cuts have reached their practical limit; any deterioration beyond budget assumptions must then be met through emergency borrowing or service reductions with adverse impacts.
findings.figures: Savings delivered in previous four years: over £20 million; new savings planned for MTFS period: £7.172 million (less than two years of current annual savings rate)
findings.quote: Given the Council's current financial position and the extensive savings delivered in recent years, the scope for further efficiencies is constrained and the savings programme has therefore been deliberately targeted and proportionate.

findings.headline: Structural funding disadvantage of approximately £25 million over three years due to revised deprivation formula in finance settlement
findings.detail: Under the revised children's services funding formula, Redcar and Cleveland was downgraded from earlier proposals due to changes to deprivation measures. The council documents that authorities which benefited most from this change have average children in care rates ranked 130th nationally—less than one-third of Redcar and Cleveland's rate—yet receive significantly higher Core Spending Power increases (averaging 30.3% versus 14 percentage points lower for Redcar and Cleveland). This structural disadvantage is not a consequence of transformation success or inefficiency, but of the national funding formula parameters.
findings.matters: A structural underfunding of this magnitude indicates the council cannot resolve its children's services financial crisis through transformation or efficiency; it requires change to the national funding formula or ongoing supplementary government support, both of which are beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Redcar and Cleveland funding formula ranking: 44th for assessed need (deterioration from earlier proposals); funding differential over settlement period: approximately £25 million; comparison authorities average CSP increase: 30.3% vs Redcar and Cleveland's 16.3%
findings.quote: For Redcar and Cleveland, each 1% of Core Spending Power equates to approximately £1.8 million, meaning this differential would equate to around £25 million of additional funding over the settlement period.

findings.headline: Schools High Needs deficit of £20.2 million forecast by end of 2025/26 with resolution dependent on conditional government grant
findings.detail: The council's SEND deficit is forecast to reach £20.2 million by end of 2025/26. The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant to resolve approximately 90% of accumulated deficits, which would address approximately £18 million of Redcar and Cleveland's deficit. However, this grant is conditional on Department for Education approval of a local SEND reform plan. The document notes 'further detail is awaited' in the Schools White Paper on how residual deficits will be addressed after the statutory override expires in March 2028, creating uncertainty about post-2028 liability.
findings.matters: A £20 million education deficit is a substantial contingent liability; while the government has signalled support, the relief is conditional (requiring DfE approval) and temporary (statutory override expires 2028), creating material future budget risk.

findings.headline: Freeport business rates growth forecasts critical to sustainability plan are subject to significant uncertainty and already slipped
findings.detail: The council's financial sustainability path depends on business rates growth from the Freeport, forecast at £24.303 million per year. A £1.948 million collection fund deficit on business rates for 2025/26 is directly attributed to 'delays on business growth within the Teesworks site', indicating forecast timing has already slipped. The council has created a Business Rates Volatility Fund to mitigate 'increased estimates for 2026/27' but this acknowledgment confirms uncertainty.
findings.matters: The council's credible path to financial sustainability is dependent on Freeport growth that is not yet confirmed and already delayed; if this growth fails to materialize as forecast, the council has no backup plan and will face acute financial distress with no reserves to absorb the impact.

findings.headline: Children's social care costs remain the dominant budget pressure with the council carrying the fifth-highest children in care rate nationally

The council has the fifth highest rate of children in care nationally yet is ranked only 44th in the revised children's services funding formula. The document states demographic and cost pressures remain 'particularly acute'. The council is attempting to manage demand through transformation activity and in-borough care market development, but acknowledges that 'further escalation can be slowed' only through successful delivery of these initiatives, indicating uncertainty about containment.
findings.matters: Children's social care is the fastest-growing cost for upper tier councils; a council with the fifth-highest demand but inadequate funding is at severe risk of further deterioration if demand rises or cost pressures accelerate.

findings.headline: Required borrowing for 2026/27 budget gap increased by 23% to £18.4 million after final finance settlement
findings.detail: The council submitted a provisional borrowing application of approximately £15 million in December 2025 based on anticipated finance settlement assumptions. After the final settlement was published in February 2026, the required borrowing increased to £18.4 million. The council is using the government's temporary scheme to capitalize revenue pressures and fund them through borrowing repayable over an extended period. This scheme is explicitly temporary, intended only to bridge short-term gaps where other options are exhausted.
findings.matters: A widening budget gap combined with depleted reserves indicates financial deterioration between forecast and outcome; temporary borrowing schemes mask underlying deficits and create material refinancing risk when flexibilities expire.
findings.figures: Provisional borrowing requirement: approximately £15 million; final borrowing requirement: £18.4 million (increase of £3.4 million or 23%)

findings.headline: General Fund balance £7.870m for 2026/27; total reserves forecast £15.844m by 31 March 2026, lower quartile of upper tier authorities

The document repeatedly emphasizes these levels as 'critically low' and notes that even when reserves were higher in 2021/22, they benchmarked in the lower quartile of upper tier authorities. This depletion reflects years of funding not keeping pace with inflation and service demand. The document explicitly warns this leaves the council 'exposed to a heightened level of financial risk' with inadequate ability to absorb shocks.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is the primary indicator of financial distress; a council with inadequate reserves cannot absorb unexpected cost spikes without emergency borrowing or service cuts, and faces significantly elevated refinancing risk.
findings.figures: General Fund balance: £7.870 million for 2026/27; total reserves forecast to be £15.844 million by 31 March 2026; reserve levels even at 2021/22 peak benchmarked in lower quartile of upper tier authorities
findings.quote: Reflecting the high degree of uncertainty within some of the key financial pressures facing the Council, and with reserves now at critically low levels, the organisation is exposed to a heightened level of financial risk.

findings.headline: Capitalised expenditure subject to 20-year asset life MRP condition

findings.matters: The 20-year MRP ceiling is restrictive and will force faster repayment of the capitalised amount than the council might otherwise assume. This affects medium-term budget planning and cash flow management.

findings.quote: Where expenditure is capitalised, the authority shall charge annual MRP using the asset life method with a proxy 'asset life' of no more than 20 years.

findings.headline: Council directed to avoid new borrowing and prioritise capital receipts for funding support
findings.detail: The Minister explicitly expects the council to avoid or minimise new borrowing to fund the support, instead using existing or future capital receipts where possible. The council should avoid asset sales that do not represent value for money and dispose of community heritage assets only where unavoidable.
findings.matters: This directive constrains the council's borrowing flexibility going forward. It signals the government's concern about debt sustainability and forces reliance on capital receipts—which may require asset disposals or create funding competition between services.

findings.matters: A capitalisation direction of this scale indicates the government recognises the council faces unmanageable financial pressures that require central intervention. It will artificially improve the council's balance sheet by converting revenue expenditure to capital, affecting borrowing position and debt sustainability.

If called and rates are reset unfavourably, the council would need to either accept higher rates or repay and refinance.
findings.matters: LOBO loans are an embedded refinancing risk that can crystallise unexpectedly. Even if the current call is unlikely, the existence of this contingency in the debt portfolio illustrates the council's exposure to interest rate movements and lender discretion—factors that concern creditors.

findings.matters: Premiums are a dead weight on the budget that consume revenue capacity without providing service benefit. They reduce the council's ability to afford essential services and future capital investment. The fact that £17.372m of existing debt is allocated to this non-productive cost matters to creditors assessing debt serviceability.

findings.quote: Premiums and discounts incurred in the restructuring of the Lender Option – Borrower Option (LOBO) and market loans... The net premium outstanding on the 31 March 2026 is £17.372 million.

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to increase by £26.922m to £263.821m in 2026/27, driven by DSG deficit and use of reserves to fund revenue pressures
findings.detail: The council's forecast external borrowing requirement is increasing by £26.922m in 2026/27 alone, on top of £20.554m in 2025/26. This acceleration reflects both the capital programme and the DSG deficit requiring debt finance. The council explicitly notes this is driven by 'the impact of the DSG deficit and the use of reserves to fund pressures in the revenue budget.'
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating borrowing, especially when driven by non-discretionary spend (DSG), signals weakening financial control. If capital borrowing is accelerating this fast, there is little room for the council to manage new pressures or invest in resilience without breaching debt limits.
findings.quote: The Council's level of external loans is anticipated to be £236.899 million at the end of 2025/26, an increase of £20.554 million on the previous year... due to funding the in-year capital investment programme less the in-year Minimum Revenue Payment, the impact of the DSG deficit and the use of reserves to fund pressures in the revenue budget.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £20m existing plus £8m additional in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council faces a growing DSG deficit, with £20m already accrued as of March 2026 and a further £8m anticipated during the coming financial year. This deficit is not part of the Capital Financing Requirement but represents real debt that impacts the council's liquidity and overall borrowing position. The council has been forced to borrow to cover this unfunded liability.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in schools funding that is unmet by government represents a contingent liability that erodes financial flexibility and requires ongoing borrowing to cover. This is particularly acute for lenders assessing whether the council can service its debts when mandatory spend on schools is outpacing funding.
findings.figures: £20.000 million on 31 March 2026 and increasing by approximately another £8.000 million during 2026/27
findings.quote: Pressures on school funding, particularly on the High Needs Block has resulted in a deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). This is anticipated to be £20.000 million on the 31 March 2026 and increasing by approximately another £8.000 million during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: Budget gap projected for 2026/27 after exhausting £20+ million in savings over four years
findings.detail: The council has delivered 'over £20 million' in savings in the last four financial years and 'even more over the past decade', yet the Medium-Term Financial Strategy now 'projecting a budget gap for 2026/27'. The CFO acknowledges 'limited scope for further savings' because of 'stretching both frontline and back-office services', indicating the council has reached the limit of what can be cut.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget pressures are cyclical (fixable through efficiency) or structural (requiring external intervention). Exhausted savings capacity and a persistent gap indicate a structural funding problem with no near-term internal solution.
findings.figures: £20 million+ savings over 4 years; projected gap for 2026/27; no identified savings solution
findings.quote: Despite the best efforts of the Authority, delivering significant levels of savings over the last four financial years (over £20 million) and even more over the past decade, the persistence and scale of pressures, particularly in high-cost children's care placements, combined with years of reducing resourcing levels through the outdated funding formula, reserves are now at a critically low level.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: Application for £15 million emergency government borrowing to cover 2026/27 budget gap
findings.detail: Unable to identify savings to balance the 2026/27 budget, the council has applied for £15 million under a government scheme that allows councils to 'capitalise revenue pressures for the coming year and fund them through borrowing, repayable over an extended period'. The CFO describes this as 'a vital bridge' to stability, but it is in essence borrowing to cover operational deficits.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council is planning to borrow to mask structural spending problems rather than balance operationally. This indicates the underlying financial position is unsustainable and borrowing is delaying, not solving, the core issue.
findings.figures: £15 million provisional application amount
findings.quote: the Authority has made an application to the Government's scheme that allows additional financial flexibilities, allowing councils to capitalise revenue pressures for the coming year and fund them through borrowing, repayable over an extended period. For Redcar and Cleveland, it would provide a vital bridge to the more stable financial position forecast within the current MTFS period. An initial assessment of the projected budget gap for 2026/27 has informed a provisional application amount of £15 million.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: £5.075 million revenue overspend in 2024/25 with £2.9 million overspend forecast for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council significantly overshot its budget, despite mitigation measures that reduced the Q1 2024/25 overspend forecast from £12.369 million. The 2025/26 position remains unbalanced, with the CFO noting the council is 'exposed to high demand pressures in children's social care which make this position more challenging'. In-year measures from 2024/25 remain in place but have not closed the gap.
findings.matters: Persistent overspending signals the council cannot live within budget and is relying on reserves to balance. This pattern raises whether future budget forecasts are realistic and suggests the underlying problem is structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: £5.075m final overspend 2024/25; £12.369m Q1 forecast; £2.9m Q2 2025/26 forecast
findings.quote: The Council did however report throughout the year on significant financial pressures in the revenue budget, particularly in relation to Children's Social Care, pay award and home-to-school transport which resulted in an eventual overspend at year end of £5.075 million.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Assurances from Director of Finance - Signed PW
findings.headline: General reserves fallen 56% from £42.717m on 31 March 2021 to £18.782m at Q2 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's general reserves have fallen sharply over four years. The CFO warns of 'the risk of reserves being depleted to an unacceptably low level' and states reserves must now 'absorb the eventual aggregate overspend position likely in 2025/26'. At the current trajectory, the council has limited buffer to absorb any service demand shock.
findings.matters: A lender assessing risk needs to know the council's financial resilience. Critically low reserves indicate limited capacity to weather unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, raising default risk significantly.
findings.figures: £42.717m (31 March 2021) to £18.782m (Q2 2025/26) — a 56% decline in four years
findings.quote: The Council has, since 2022/23 experienced a reduction in reserves from a high point on 31 March 2021 of £42.717m, to a latest reserves position at Quarter 2 of 2025/26 of £18.782 million, which will also need to absorb the eventual aggregate overspend position likely in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Authority's long-term financial self-sustainability objective is now conditional on trade deal implementation and timing
findings.detail: The authority's stated strategic aim is to become self-sufficient and operate within fees and charges collected. However, delivery of this objective is now explicitly conditional on how the trade deal is implemented. The 2026/27 budget shows a £207k surplus before member council contributions, but this is contingent on POAO income continuing at 2025/26 levels.
findings.matters: If self-sufficiency cannot be achieved, member councils (including Redcar and Cleveland) will need to increase their Riparian contributions indefinitely; the medium-term financial plan is currently not committed beyond 2026/27 pending trade deal clarity
findings.figures: £207k estimated surplus in 2026/27; Riparian contributions held at £157,650 (unchanged from 2025/26)
findings.quote: A long-term financial aim of the RTPHA remains to become more self-sustainable and operate within the fees and charges it collects to cover its operational costs and overheads. The draft 26/27 budget implies a surplus before Riparian contributions. The delivery of this objective continue to be closely assessed as the new EU Trade Deal is implemented.

findings.headline: Authority plans £175k reserve distribution in 2025/26 specifically to absorb anticipated trade deal impact
findings.detail: The authority is planning to distribute £175k of reserves in 2025/26, bringing estimated closing reserves to c.£563k. This distribution is explicitly made with knowledge that the trade deal will reduce both income and recurring costs. The reserve level is intended to cover costs associated with reducing operations and provide buffer against unbudgeted costs.
findings.matters: Shows the authority is proactively managing a known severe risk; also signals that operational downsizing is being planned and budgeted for
findings.figures: £175k planned distribution in 2025/26; c.£563k estimated closing reserves after distribution; current general reserves £380k
findings.quote: Given the knowledge that a new trade deal is to be introduced, which will reduce income and recurring costs it is suggested that a distribution of reserves is applied in 2025/26 for £175,000.

findings.headline: Authority is heavily reliant on a single customer for its primary income stream
findings.detail: The authority explicitly notes that it is heavily reliant on one main customer for Product of Animal Origin income. This concentration risk is flagged as a reason for maintaining elevated reserves and monitoring income levels closely.
findings.matters: Loss or change in behaviour of this one customer would be catastrophic; income volatility would be severe and uncontrollable by the authority
findings.figures: One customer dependency for POAO income; POAO budgeted at c.£65k per month
findings.quote: The Authority is heavily reliant on one main customer regarding Product of Animal Original Income.

findings.headline: EU trade deal will eliminate the majority of Product of Animal Origin income from April 2027
findings.detail: A new trade deal announced in 2025 is expected to result in the majority of Product of Animal Origin income ceasing once implemented. Implementation is expected earliest from 1 April 2027, after the 2026/27 financial year. The authority has begun reviewing and costing associated delivery cost reductions, but the exact impact remains uncertain.
findings.matters: POAO is budgeted at c.£65k per month and is a material income stream for this small authority; loss of it will force higher contributions from member councils including Redcar and Cleveland, or trigger operational downsizing
findings.figures: c.£65k income per month budgeted for POAO in 2026/27; implementation expected earliest 01 April 2027
findings.quote: A new trade deal was announced with the EU during 2025. It is anticipated this will result in the majority of Product of Animal Origin income ceasing once implemented.

findings.headline: Financial forecast contingent on EU trade policy and border operations remaining unchanged
findings.detail: The authority explicitly notes that the forecast 'assumes that the Governments announcement regarding a trade deal with the EU earlier in the year, and expected change to the Border Target Operating Model, has no impact on the 2025/26 financial year'. This is a material assumption underpinning both the income and cost forecasts.
findings.matters: Changes to EU trade terms or Border Target Operating Model implementation would directly affect animal product income (the main upside variance) and veterinary costs, creating material downside risk to the reserve and surplus projections
findings.figures: No figures; policy assumption flagged but not quantified
findings.quote: The forecast assumes that the Governments announcement regarding a trade deal with the EU earlier in the year, and expected change to the Border Target Operating Model, has no impact on the 2025/26 financial year given the relatively short time frame now remaining.

findings.headline: Reserves projected to increase from £380k to £738k, nearly doubling opening balance
findings.detail: Estimated reserves balance at 31 March 2026 is £737,919 compared to opening balance of £380,414, driven by a projected surplus of £199,855 plus Riparian contributions of £157,650. This significant improvement strengthens the authority's financial position.
findings.matters: A doubling of reserves materially improves the authority's financial resilience and creditworthiness, reducing future borrowing needs and demonstrating operational financial strength
findings.figures: Opening balance 1 April 2025: £380,414; estimated balance 31 March 2026: £737,919; estimated surplus: £199,855
findings.quote: Reserves are projected to increase from their opening balance of £380,414 to around £738,000 (including current surplus and Riparian contributions).

findings.headline: Additional veterinary costs of £25,000 driven by EU animal disease outbreaks affecting border operations
findings.detail: The authority is incurring unbudgeted demand-driven costs of £25,000 for additional veterinary service provision to handle increased checks following animal disease outbreaks in the EU. The paper states this 'will continue to be monitored as the year progresses', indicating ongoing exposure.
findings.matters: This demonstrates operational cost exposure to external disease events affecting border traffic and supply chain disruption, with material cost implications that extend beyond 2025/26 if disease persists
findings.figures: Additional veterinary service provision: £25,000
findings.quote: additional veterinary service provision (£25,000) to cover the increase in checks following the outbreaks of animal related diseases in the EU

findings.headline: Product of animal origin income nearly five times higher than budget due to largely unknown source at time of budget setting
findings.detail: The authority budgeted £48k but is forecasting £236k in product of animal origin income—a £188k variance. The paper notes this reflects 'increased income achieved in year' that was not anticipated when the 2025/26 budget was approved in December 2024. This volatility is material to the authority's financial position.
findings.matters: A £240k income variance represents a significant and unplanned positive swing that indicates either budget weakness or a material change in the underlying service (Border Target Operating Model implementation), affecting financial predictability
findings.figures: Product of animal origin: £236k actual vs £48k budget; total income variance £240,305
findings.quote: The forecast income and costs for 25/26 have been updated for increased run rate on product of animal origin income (c £236k, Sept 25 forecast: £48k) to reflect increased income achieved in year.

findings.headline: Collection fund deficit of £1.016m from prior year, with current year position dependent on property growth to offset collection pressures
findings.detail: The 2024/25 collection fund closed with a £1.016m deficit due to higher bad debt provisions and growth in council tax support and exemptions. For 2025/26, the council is estimating a £0.278m net deficit after accounting for projected property growth; without the growth benefit (£0.738m), the underlying deficit would be worse.
findings.matters: The underlying revenue collection position is weaker than the net figures suggest, with property growth effectively masking ongoing collection challenges. The sustainability of property growth is uncertain.
findings.figures: 2024/25 deficit £1.016m; 2025/26 estimated gross deficit offset by £0.738m growth benefit, leaving £0.278m net deficit
findings.quote: This was due to growth in discounts, exemption and council tax support in the second half of the financial year and a higher contribution to the bad debt provision than estimated.

findings.headline: Bad debt provision contribution has nearly doubled from £879k to £1.532m, flagged as higher than anticipated
findings.detail: The council's contribution to the collection fund bad debt provision increased materially year-on-year from £879k in 2024/25 to £1.532m in 2025/26. This reflects both prior-year collection performance worse than expected and anticipated collection challenges for the current year. The prior-year increase was driven by growth in discounts, exemptions and council tax support combined with higher-than-estimated bad debt provisions.
findings.matters: A material increase in bad debt provisions indicates worsening collection experience or anticipated delinquency. For a lender, this signals either household financial stress in the borough or collection challenges—both material to council financial resilience.
findings.figures: £1.532 million (2025/26) vs £879k (2024/25); prior year deficit attributed to this provision was £1.016 million
findings.quote: higher contribution to the bad debt provision than estimated

findings.headline: Business rates collection deficit of £3.406m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council faces a significant business rates pressure in 2026/27 combining two elements: a £0.443m deficit on the collection fund (the council's 49% share) and a £2.963m pressure from reduced designated income connected to Teesworks reprofiling. This £3.406m total must be factored into the 2026/27 budget. The deficit arose from worsening 2024/25 outturn and a reduction in liability due to reprofiling of growth on Teesworks.
findings.matters: A £3.4m income loss in a single year represents a material pressure on a council already at the borrowing scheme threshold. While the council expects future growth from Freeport regeneration, the timing and quantum remain subject to risk.
findings.figures: £3.406 million total (£0.443m collection fund deficit + £2.963m designated income pressure)
findings.quote: The total deficit to factor in is therefore the deficit on the collection fund of £0.443 million and the pressure on designated income of £2.963 million giving a total of £3.406 million on the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Children's social care costs rising with £4m per annum ongoing investment needed
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demographic and cost pressures in children's services. The number of children in care has increased with higher complexity requiring more expensive residential and supported accommodation placements, compounded by market insufficiency. The council has modelled demand and set aside a growth allocation to contain increases within £4m per annum from 2026/27 onwards. Additional £3m capital investment is planned over two years for in-borough accommodation development.
findings.matters: Persistent high-cost children's social care demand is a core driver of the council's financial distress and budget gap. This is not a transitory pressure; the council projects £4m annual growth indefinitely, suggesting structural service cost increases.
findings.figures: £4 million per annum growth allocation from 2026/27; £3 million capital investment over two years for in-borough placements
findings.quote: The number of children in care has increased, with a significant increase in complexity requiring a higher proportion of more expensive residential and supported accommodation placements, the costs of which have been compounded by market insufficiency.

findings.headline: £15m government borrowing scheme application required to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council is applying for participation in the government's Additional Financial Flexibilities scheme, which allows councils to capitalise revenue pressures and fund them through borrowing repayable over extended periods. An initial budget gap assessment has informed a provisional application of £15m. The scheme requires external assurance from MHCLG with review in early January and final approval anticipated in February. The council states this is a bridge to a more sustainable position forecast within the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Dependency on a government exceptional finance scheme signals acute financial distress and indicates the council cannot balance its budget through normal income and savings. Scheme approval is not yet confirmed and timeline aligns with budget-setting, creating implementation risk.
findings.figures: £15 million provisional application amount
findings.quote: An initial assessment of the projected budget gap for 2026/27 has informed a provisional application amount of £15 million... allowing councils to capitalise revenue pressures for the coming year and fund them through borrowing, repayable over an extended period.

findings.headline: MTFS reserve forecast at £6.063m (2026/27) and £3.834m (2027/28) with reserves described as at critically low levels
findings.detail: The council has depleted reserves through sustained budget pressures over recent years. The paper explicitly states reserves are now at critically low levels. For 2026/27, only £6m of projected business rates growth is being allocated to rebuild the MTFS reserve, which will operate as a budget smoothing mechanism. The MTFS reserve is forecast to reach only £6.063m at the end of 2026/27.
findings.matters: Critically depleted reserves mean the council has minimal buffer to absorb adverse financial developments or service demand changes, which is a key financial resilience indicator for lenders.
findings.figures: MTFS reserve forecast £6.063m (2026/27), £3.834m (2027/28)
findings.quote: with reserves at critically low levels, there is a need to rebuild reserves, both immediately and incrementally over the MTFS period to provide sufficient resilience to support the management of risks in the delivery of the revenue budget

findings.detail: The council's planned e-tendering system (OPEN) is supposed to provide spend data and analysis capability to inform procurement decisions. This module remains undelivered with no expected delivery date, while the supplier focuses on core tendering functionality and bug fixes.
findings.matters: Without spend visibility, the council lacks financial controls over its third-party spend and cannot easily identify cost savings or manage supplier spend efficiently. This is a governance and control risk.

findings.headline: Business rates and council tax collection rates both declining year-on-year
findings.detail: Business rates collection at 65.61% by end of October, down from 66.05% the previous year. Council tax collection at 60.32%, down from 60.7% the previous year. Both metrics track whether the council can convert its tax base into cash.

findings.headline: Teesside Pension Fund auditor issued disclaimed opinion on 2023/24 accounts, forcing council audit opinion modification and creating ongoing valuation uncertainty
findings.detail: The Teesside Pension Fund auditor was unable to complete asset valuations before the 28 February 2025 backstop date and issued a disclaimed opinion on the fund's 2023/24 financial statements. This forced the council's auditors to modify their 2023/24 opinion. Further assurance will not be available until January/February 2026. Pension liabilities are material on the council's balance sheet and involve complex actuarial estimates.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities represent one of the council's largest balance sheet items. Valuation uncertainty means the true financial position may not be accurately reflected in the accounts.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinion issued February 2025 for 2023/24; assurance expected January/February 2026
findings.quote: This lack of assurance meant that we modified our audit opinion in 2023/24 for the Council to reflect this

findings.paper_title: 5. RCBC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 24-25 FINAL 14-11-25
findings.headline: Council achieved only 88% of 2024/25 efficiency savings target and now faces demands for £15.8m of new savings over two years
findings.detail: The council delivered £6.672m of a £7.574m (88%) efficiency savings target in 2024/25, continuing a pattern of shortfall (91% in 2023/24, 83% in 2022/23). The 2025/26 MTFP requires £8.8m in savings; the Q1 report indicates a further £7m of transformation savings are needed for 2026/27 to bridge funding gaps. The auditor notes 'the scale of required savings in 2025/26 and 2026/27 presents a considerable challenge.'
findings.matters: If the council cannot reliably deliver planned savings at scale, its financial position will worsen faster than forecast. The auditor is flagging concern about achievability, not confidence.
findings.figures: £6.672m of £7.574m achieved 2024/25 (88%); £8.8m target 2025/26; £7m transformation savings needed 2026/27
findings.quote: the scale of required savings in 2025/26 and 2026/27 presents a considerable challenge

findings.paper_title: 5. RCBC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 24-25 FINAL 14-11-25
findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 shows £2.674m forecast overspend and £18.2m adverse variance from original MTFP, driven by £30m reduction in Teesworks business rates income
findings.detail: The revised 2025/26 MTFP contains a £18.2m adverse variance compared to the forecast made in February 2025. The largest single change is a reduction of circa £30m in projected business rates from Teesworks sites due to delayed openings and revised valuation office assessments. The Council is also facing £5.2m shortfall in transformation savings and wider income variances of £10.1m. Q1 forecasts a £2.674m overspend, forcing an unplanned £1.736m drawdown from reserves instead of the planned £0.934m contribution.
findings.matters: The council's financial plan has deteriorated significantly in the first quarter, showing that assumptions made in February have already proven too optimistic. Teesworks delays are a specific new risk and a material income shock.
findings.figures: £18.2m adverse variance in revised MTFP; £30m reduction in Teesworks projections; £5.2m transformation savings shortfall; £2.674m Q1 2025/26 forecast overspend; £1.736m actual reserve drawdown vs £0.934m planned
findings.quote: Delays in some sites' opening plus revised information on likely valuations of the sites by the Valuation Office has required projections to be significantly reduced by circa £30 million over the MTFP

findings.paper_title: 5. RCBC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 24-25 FINAL 14-11-25
findings.headline: Children in Care overspends of £12.8m in 2024/25 persist despite £11m additional budget investment, with Q1 2025/26 showing £2.6m new overspend
findings.detail: Children in Care costs have overrun by approximately £10m per year for the past three years. The council increased the base budget by £7m in 2024/25 and a further £4m in 2025/26, but the service still overran by £12.8m in 2024/25 (including an £11.1m overspend on residential placements). Q1 2025/26 is already showing a £2.6m overspend, driven by 20 additional placements in the first three months and market insufficiency for placement types needed.
findings.matters: This is a demand-led service where budget increases are not solving the underlying cost pressure. The auditor flags this as unsustainable and a threat to reserves. It suggests either need growth or cost drivers are beyond the council's control.

findings.quote: This has not been enough to avoid further overspends in 2025/26 of circa £2.6 million in quarter 1

findings.paper_title: 5. RCBC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 24-25 FINAL 14-11-25
findings.headline: Council reserves fell from £42.7m in 2021/22 to £17.6m in 2024/25 and are projected to reach £10.2m by March 2027
findings.detail: Usable reserves declined from £42.7m in 2021/22 to £17.6m in 2024/25 and are projected to fall further to £10.2m by March 2027. The general fund balance remains at the minimum threshold of £6.6m; the remainder is earmarked for specific future commitments and not available to cover unexpected pressures. The auditor explicitly notes this level is 'low for a Council of this size, complexity and risks it is facing.'
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council has minimal buffer to absorb service pressures, demand spikes, or funding shortfalls. This reduces financial flexibility and resilience.
